source.title: Weight-sparse transformers have interpretable circuits
source.authors: Leo Gao; Achyuta Rajaram; Jacob Coxon; Soham V. Govande; Bowen Baker; Daniel P. Mossing

record.file_problem: The text contains some control-character, page-layout, and figure-extraction artifacts, but the full paper and appendices are present and readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies weight sparsity and examines circuit compactness and feature quality. It reports that sparse models are more interpretable by its metrics, while some features remain polysemantic or smeared across nodes, refining rather than directly testing the toy-model geometry claim.
record.gate_note: The study does not test the original toy-model setup or directly measure overlapping directions, feature sparsity, or importance-based dimension allocation. Compact circuit size and activation kurtosis are related evidence, not measurements of those geometries. Cited results from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: Superposition is the motivation for weight-sparse training, not the object of measurement. The paper reports only its own method's results: circuit size versus dense models, the capability-interpretability frontier, residual-stream kurtosis, binarizability and bridge steering. Residual polysemanticity comes up in Limitations as qualitative remarks, with no rate, no capacity or importance manipulation, and no feature-geometry measurement. Weight sparsity is a training constraint imposed on purpose, so nothing here tests the capacity account (V2) or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that weight-sparse transformers have much smaller, human-understandable task circuits (about 16x smaller than loss-matched dense models). Sparser weights trade capability for interpretability, while scaling width improves the frontier. Scaling beyond tens of millions of nonzero parameters remains hard. Bridges give preliminary results for explaining dense models. They acknowledge residual polysemanticity and imperfect faithfulness (mean ablation rather than causal scrubbing), and speculate that a little superposition may be advantageous or that wider models could resolve it.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains weight-sparse transformers and prunes task-specific circuits; it does not reproduce the toy-model feature-vector setup or its geometry measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Weight L0 and total parameter count change the capability-interpretability frontier; the authors also report activation sparsity changes with weight sparsity and model size.

fits_no_version.finding: In weight-sparse models, concepts are still smeared across several nodes that also serve other tasks, though less than in dense models. Some nodes are exactly monosemantic and others are not (qualitative, no rate).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Imposed weight sparsity reduces but does not eliminate polysemanticity in small transformers.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight-sparse models yield task circuits roughly 16x smaller than loss-matched dense models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight sparsity yields more compact task circuits at matched pretraining loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Residual-stream kurtosis rises as weight L0 shrinks or total parameter count grows (Fig. 10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight sparsity induces activation sparsity in the residual stream.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed L0, larger models improve both capability and circuit size; lowering L0 trades capability for interpretability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model width and weight sparsity shape the capability-interpretability frontier differently.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight sparsity allows a larger activation L0 without collapsing into polysemantic features. Too much activation sparsity becomes Pareto-dominated (Fig. 37, Sec. 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight sparsity and activation sparsity interact in determining feature monosemanticity.

record.problems: The task suite consists of 20 handcrafted Python binary-prediction tasks. Qualitative circuit interpretations cover three tasks across two models. Circuit faithfulness relies mainly on mean ablation; the authors state it is weaker than full causal scrubbing. The paper also notes residual polysemanticity and limitations in scaling to complex tasks.

untested.parts: No toy model, no sparsity-dependent transition, no measurement of feature geometry.
No measurement of feature importance, of dedicated versus shared dimensions, or of capacity-driven polysemanticity.
No test of polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
No measurement of how features spread across neurons in dense LLMs. The bridges are SAE-like, but recovery of sparse features is not evaluated as evidence for superposition.
SAE features are not assessed for completeness, stability or canonicity.
Feature dimensionality is not tested. Non-binary feature magnitudes are not the same question.

missing.what: Activation-sparsity sweep (Fig. 37): weight sparsity permits larger activation L0 without polysemantic collapse. It bears on no version, but no row records it.
Cross-layer superposition check: replacing channel 1249 with a linear function of layer-2 activation costs 7e-4 versus 4e-3 nats. The authors conclude it is redundancy, not superposition.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T5' and its V2 limits_scope label are not supported. The study's polysemanticity remarks are qualitative limitations of its own method under an imposed sparsity constraint, not a measurement of capacity-driven polysemanticity. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions, the feature-sparsity transition, or regular overlap geometry.
Examines circuit compactness and qualitative polysemanticity under weight sparsity, but does not measure feature importance, dedicated dimensions, or the proposed allocation mechanism directly.
Does not test polysemanticity in the absence of capacity pressure or whether polysemanticity alone evidences superposition.
Does not measure feature spread across neurons in real LLMs or test SAE recovery of sparse features.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Does not test whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.

rows.subject: weight-sparse model (compared with dense model)
rows.operation_detail: Compared minimal task-circuit size at matched pretraining loss, averaged across hand-curated tasks.
rows.measure: Geometric mean number of edges in the circuit; sparse-model circuits are roughly 16-fold smaller at a given loss.
rows.baseline: Dense model at the same pretraining loss
rows.note: Circuit compactness is used as an interpretability metric; it does not directly measure feature overlap or neuron polysemanticity.
rows.check: This is the study's own method compared with dense models (circuit-size interpretability proxy). It belongs under method performance, not under the claim.

rows.subject: weight-sparse models (aggregate; specific model names not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Qualitatively examined polysemantic features in the models' circuits.
rows.measure: Whether features or concepts are smeared across nodes that also perform other tasks.
rows.baseline: Dense models are described as having this to a greater extent
rows.value: Some features remain polysemantic: concepts are smeared across multiple nodes that also perform other tasks, though less than in dense models.
rows.locator: Section 5, Limitations and Future Work: Polysemantic features
rows.note: The authors suggest this could reflect an advantage to a small amount of superposition or could be resolved by scaling width; the study does not isolate the mechanism.
rows.check: A qualitative remark in the Limitations section about weight-sparse models, with no count or rate and nothing tying smearing to capacity competition or feature importance. It does not measure V2's mechanism. The only baseline is the vague 'much lesser extent than dense models'.

rows.subject: weight-sparse models (aggregate; specific model names not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Checked node interpretations on the pretraining distribution.

conditions.value: some nodes; one illustrated node is explicitly cherry-picked

rows.value: Some, but not all, nodes are exactly monosemantic; the illustrated node is described as cherry-picked.
rows.note: This reports residual polysemanticity but does not measure feature importance or capacity allocation.
rows.check: The statement 'some but not all nodes are exactly monosemantic' rests on a cherry-picked node (Fig. 39), with no proportion reported. It says nothing about capacity allocation, so it does not bear on V2.

rows.subject: weight-sparse models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured residual-stream activation sparsity using kurtosis while varying weight sparsity and model size.
rows.value: Kurtosis increases as weight L0 gets smaller or total parameter count gets larger.
rows.note: The paper says residual-stream entries are rarely exactly zero and uses kurtosis as a sparsity measure; this is not a measurement of overlapping feature directions.

rows.subject: weight-sparse models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Varied weight L0 and total parameter count and measured the capability-interpretability frontier.

conditions.value: varied; moving L0 trades off capability and interpretability

rows.measure: Pretraining loss as capability and pruned circuit size as interpretability.
rows.value: Increasing model size at fixed L0 improves both capability and interpretability; changing L0 moves along the frontier, trading them off.
rows.note: These are the paper's capability and circuit-size results, not a direct test of feature competition or geometry.
rows.check: Method performance only: the capability-interpretability frontier under L0 and width scaling.
